title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: The newly elected marshal and many of the winning party dined that day at Vronsky's.

Vronsky had come to the elections partly because he was bored in the country and wanted to show Anna his right to independence, and also to repay Sviazhsky for the trouble he had taken on his behalf at the district council election by supporting him here — but chiefly in order to discharge to the letter all those duties of a nobleman and landowner he had taken on. He hadn't expected in the least that the election would so interest him, would excite him so keenly, or that he would be so good at this kind of thing. He was a complete newcomer to the circle of provincial nobility, but his success was unmistakable, and he wasn't wrong in supposing he had already gained a certain influence. This influence was due to his wealth and his reputation, the capital town house lent to him by his old friend Shirkov — who held a post in the department of finances and was director of a flourishing bank in Kashin; the excellent cook Vronsky had brought from the country; and his friendship with the governor, an old schoolfellow of his — and one he had patronized and protected, at that. But more than anything, what contributed to his success was his direct, even-tempered manner with everyone, which quickly made most of the noblemen reverse the current opinion that he was haughty. He was conscious himself that — apart from that whimsical gentleman married to Kitty Shtcherbatskaya, who had _à propos de bottes_ poured out a flood of irrelevant absurdities with such venomous fury — every nobleman he had gotten to know had come over to his side. He saw clearly, and other people saw it too, that he had done a great deal to secure Nevyedovsky's success. And now, at his own table, celebrating Nevyedovsky's election, he felt an agreeable sense of triumph over the success of his candidate. The election itself had so fascinated him that, if he could manage to be married within the next three years, he was beginning to think of standing himself — much as after winning a race ridden by a jockey, he had wanted to ride a race himself.

Today he was celebrating his jockey's success. Vronsky sat at the head of the table; on his right hand sat the young governor, a general of high rank. To everyone else he was the chief man in the province, who had solemnly opened the elections with his speech and had inspired respect and even awe in many — as Vronsky could see; to Vronsky he was little Katka Maslov — that had been his nickname in the Pages' Corps — and Vronsky could tell he was shy and tried to _mettre à son aise_. On the left sat Nevyedovsky with his youthful, stubborn, malicious face. With him Vronsky was straightforward and respectful.

Sviazhsky took his defeat very lightly. As he said himself, raising his glass to Nevyedovsky, it wasn't a defeat at all in his eyes; they couldn't have found a better representative of the new direction the nobility ought to follow. And so every honest person, he said, was on the side of today's success and was rejoicing over it.

Stepan Arkadyevitch was glad too — glad he was having a good time, and that everyone was pleased. The election affair made an excellent occasion for a first-rate dinner. Sviazhsky comically imitated the marshal's tearful speech, and observed, addressing Nevyedovsky, that his excellency would have to come up with some other, more complicated method of auditing the accounts than tears. Another nobleman jokingly described how footmen in stockings had been ordered for the marshal's ball, and how now they would have to be sent back unless the new marshal would give a ball with footmen in stockings.
Throughout dinner they kept calling Nevyedovsky "our marshal" and "your excellency."

It was said with the same pleasure with which a bride is called "Madame" and her husband's name. Nevyedovsky affected to be not merely indifferent to the title but scornful of it, though it was obvious he was delighted, and had to keep himself in check so as not to give away the kind of triumph that didn't fit the new liberal tone.

After dinner several telegrams were sent off to people interested in the outcome. And Stepan Arkadyevitch, in high good humor, sent Darya Alexandrovna a telegram: "Nevyedovsky elected by twenty votes. Congratulations. Pass it on." He dictated it aloud, saying, "We must let them share in our rejoicing." Darya Alexandrovna, when she got the message, simply sighed over the rouble wasted on it, and understood that it was an after-dinner affair. She knew Stiva had a weakness after dining for _faire jouer le télégraphe._

Everything — including the excellent dinner and the wine, not from Russian merchants but imported direct from abroad — was extremely dignified, simple, and enjoyable. The party — about twenty — had been picked by Sviazhsky from among the more active new liberals, all of the same way of thinking, who were at the same time clever and well bred. They drank, half jokingly, to the health of the new marshal of the province, of the governor, of the bank director, and of "our amiable host."
Vronsky was satisfied. He had never expected to find so pleasant a tone in the provinces.

Toward the end of dinner things were livelier still. The governor invited Vronsky to come to a concert for the benefit of the Servians, which his wife — eager to make his acquaintance — had been organizing.
"There'll be a ball, and you'll see the belle of the province. Worth seeing, really."
"Not in my line," Vronsky answered. He liked that English phrase. But he smiled, and promised to come.
Just before they got up from the table, while everyone was smoking, Vronsky's valet came up to him with a letter on a tray.
"From Vozdvizhenskoe by special messenger," he said with a significant expression.
"Astonishing — how like he is to the deputy prosecutor Sventitsky," one of the guests said in French of the valet, while Vronsky, frowning, read the letter.

The letter was from Anna. Before he read it, he knew what was in it. Expecting the elections to be over in five days, he had promised to be back on Friday. Today was Saturday, and he knew the letter contained reproaches for not being back at the time he had set. The letter he'd sent the evening before had probably not reached her yet.

The letter was what he had expected, but the form of it was unexpected, and particularly unpleasant to him. "Annie is very ill, the doctor says it may be inflammation. I am losing my head all alone. Princess Varvara is no help, only a hindrance. I expected you the day before yesterday, and yesterday, and now I am sending to find out where you are and what you are doing. I wanted to come myself, but thought better of it, knowing you would dislike it. Send some answer, so that I may know what to do."
The child ill — and yet she had thought of coming herself. Their daughter ill, and this hostile tone.
The innocent festivities over the election, and this gloomy, burdensome love he had to go back to, struck Vronsky by the contrast. But he had to go, and he set off home by the first train that night.
